# Navigating the Storm: US–China Tariffs' Impact on Logistics

First listed: 2025-05-05 | Evaluation cutoff: 2026-11-10

[Back to library](../README.md)

## Source versions

- [YouTube: Navigating the Storm: US–China Tariffs' Impact on Logistics](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N6ku3_zw3v0) - 2025-05-05

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Fuller maps the tariff shock from Chinese orders through ports, trucking, inventories and retail. Eisman probes denominators and challenges exaggerated claims that partial disruptions mean a complete stop. The interview distinguishes immediate freight-sector pain from later shortages, but its near-zero probability of a quick China agreement failed within twelve days. Conditional shortage and earnings scenarios require more care because policy changed. Fuller's extreme domestic-food share and net-food-exporter premises conflict with official data, while the proprietary freight statistics remain unverified.

Useful operational transmission analysis and explicit scope challenges coexist with a failed near-term political forecast and weakly verified freight extrapolations. Guest claims are kept separate from Eisman's scorecard.

<a id="youtube-N6ku3_zw3v0-c018"></a>
### 018. Products with 30-40% gross margins cannot absorb a 145% tariff on their existing cost base without price or sourcing changes.

**Right** | Craig Fuller | explanation | major

[Source at 22:10-22:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N6ku3_zw3v0&t=1330s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Under the stated illustrative assumptions, the added duty exceeds gross profit.

Qualification: Not a measured claim that all retailers have these margins; tariff base is customs value, not retail price.

Conditional reasoning: For price P and imported cost C=(1-g)P, with g=.30 to .40, duty 1.45C=.87P to 1.015P exceeds original gross profit .30P to .40P. This requires customs value to equal the assumed imported cost and no offsetting adjustment.

Assessment test: Verify customs value and retail-cost relationships for actual products.

<a id="youtube-N6ku3_zw3v0-c038"></a>
### 038. Approximately 95-98% of food consumed in the United States is made domestically.

**Wrong** | Craig Fuller | material factual premise | major

[Source at 35:09-35:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N6ku3_zw3v0&t=2109s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

FDA describes approximately 15% of overall food supply as imported; USDA estimates 15% of food-and-beverage purchases are direct imports. Neither supports 95-98% domestic supply.

Qualification: The US can be predominantly self-supplying without the claimed extreme percentage being accurate; no calorie share was supplied.

Assessment test: Specify supply, spending, calories or tonnage rather than interchange denominators.

- [Strategy for the Safety of Imported Food](https://www.fda.gov/media/120585/download?attachment=) (2019): FDA describes approximately 15% of the overall US food supply as imported, far above the 2-5% implied in the interview. The document predates the episode.
- [Food import spending shares](https://ers.usda.gov/data-products/charts-of-note/112543) (2025-05-15): Direct imports were 15% of 2023 food and beverage purchases; 85% came through domestic production, which also included imported inputs. This spending denominator is not a calorie measure.

<a id="youtube-N6ku3_zw3v0-c039"></a>
### 039. The United States is a net food exporter.

**Wrong** | Craig Fuller | material factual premise | major

[Source at 35:20-35:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N6ku3_zw3v0&t=2120s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

In 2024 the food, feed and beverage trade category had about a $50.8 billion deficit. USDA agriculture also had a deficit but is a separate denominator.

Qualification: Verdict uses standard trade-value interpretation, not an unstated calorie or tonnage balance.

Assessment test: Use a defined value category and period; do not infer food security from a trade balance.

- [December and annual 2024 trade tables](https://www.census.gov/foreign-trade/Press-Release/ft900/ft900_2412.pdf) (2025-02-05): The 2024 food, feed and beverage category shows exports of $165.256 billion and imports of $216.058 billion. Goods trade with China was approximately $143.5 billion of exports and $438.9 billion of imports. These are value measures, not calories or tonnage.
- [May agricultural trade outlook](https://ers.usda.gov/sites/default/files/_laserfiche/outlooks/112707/AES-132.pdf?v=32518) (2025-05-29): Fiscal 2024 agricultural exports were $174.4 billion and imports $206.2 billion. Agriculture is a different category from food, so this deficit is supporting context rather than the food-supply denominator.

## Framework and tools

- Trace orders, production, bookings, arrival, warehouses and retail inventories separately.
- Distinguish partial sector declines from complete economic cessation.
- Separate import-accounting effects, survey sentiment and measured activity.
- Keep the no-agreement counterfactual separate from an explicit probability forecast.
- Check denominator consistency when moving from logistics jobs to trucking jobs.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- FreightWaves high-frequency booking and truckload data, not reproduced in the episode.
- China-US container bookings versus prior baseline and year earlier.
- Apollo economist's supply-chain recession timeline.
- GDP import contribution and survey comparisons.
